newsitem.title: FINLAND: SDP'S TUOMIOJA SAYS GOVT WILL WIN CONFIDENCE VOTE.
newsitem.headline: SDP'S TUOMIOJA SAYS GOVT WILL WIN CONFIDENCE VOTE.

text.p: Erkki Tuomioja, chairman of the parliamentary group of the Social Democratic Party, the biggest group in parliament and government, said on Friday it was certain that the coalition would win the coming confidence vote.
"It certainly will," Tuomioja told Reuters by telephone in response to a question. "Nobody has stepped forward to announce an intention to topple the government."

Tuomioja declined comment on details of a compromise to be sought in talks later on Friday between leaders of the parliamentary groups of the five coalition parties on a proposal to extend retail stores' rights to keep open on Sundays.
"It is likely that we will reach quite broad consensus," he said.

Prime Minister Paavo Lipponen, also SDP chairman, said on January 30 he expected the government parties' parliamentary groups to have "genuine will to reach a consensus solution behind which all government parties could stand".

Lipponen called the confidence vote late last year after the bill to liberalise opening hours for retail stores, hairdressers and barbers was defeated in parliament. The bill was narrowly rejected, by 84 votes to 82. Of the five government parties' 142 MPs, 36 voted against the proposal, 20 of those were SDP MPs.

The confidence vote will not be just about opening hours but will also test MPs' faith in policies waiting ahead, Finance Minister Sauli Niinisto, chairman of the coalition's second biggest party, the conservatives, said in January.
Niinisto said there had been last autumn "clear mistrust" in government policy within the parliamentary groups of government parties.
That is why it had been appropriate to put confidence to the test, he said.
The confidence vote will be the fifth since the five-party rainbow coalition took office in April 1995.
Political analysts have said the Lipponen cabinet's first significant setback in parliament was an indication of growing criticism among left-wing MPs of right-leaning fiscal austerity policies.
The rejection of the Suday open bill also highlighted the influence in the SDP camp of MPs with strong trade union ties, they say.
Many unions quietly support the shop workers' union, which is fiercely opposed to liberalised retail store opening hours.

Analysts regard union support for the government's outspoken goal to see Finland among the first to enter the third stage of Economic and Monetary Union in 1999 as crucial to ensure that the SDP parliamentary group will back the project.
Parliament is scheduled to vote late in 1997 or early in 1998 whether Finland should take part in EMU.
